prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and international trade reshape labour demand, wage inequality and the adjustment of local labour markets

statement.case_for: B006 combines a conceptual framework (tasks, skill-biased change, the race between education and technology) with credible local-labour-market evidence on import competition. The China-shock designs changed how economists measure adjustment costs, and the task framework is now standard well beyond labour economics. Both strands have been replicated, extended to other countries and debated for a decade or more, so confirmation is not the issue. The topic links to my own field. Structural change, firm reallocation and growth all depend on how labour reallocates across tasks, sectors and places, and this literature is among the best-identified evidence on that margin. I still apply the same criteria as for every other field, which means scientific novelty, credibility of identification, breadth of influence and maturity. On those criteria B006 compares well with any alternative on the shortlist.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution under a three-name cap. Dorn is a core co-author of the China-shock papers. Levy and Murnane, who co-developed the task approach, are not on the ballot at all. Katz's skill-premium and education-technology work overlaps with themes the Committee has already recognised in adjacent prizes. The magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the inference properties of shift-share designs, remain contested. A single citation could therefore read as bundling two strands, technology and trade, whose credit is distributed differently.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B032 (Kiyotaki and Moore) first. His case is that collateral constraints turning small shocks into persistent, amplified fluctuations is a foundational and mature mechanism, validated by the 2007-09 crisis and not covered by the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises.
responses.response: I accept that the credit-cycles mechanism is foundational, that its attribution to Kiyotaki and Moore is unusually clean, and that it is distinct from the Bernanke-Diamond-Dybvig contribution. The case is substantive and I do not dismiss it. My reservation is empirical. As Hassler's own opening and Fredriksson's note, the quantification is still debated and most of the confirmation is indirect. B006 rests on directly identified evidence, which is why I rank it higher. I would reconsider if colleagues can point to direct tests of the amplification channel that I am underweighting.

responses.point: Enflo supports B006 but notes that Dorn is a central co-author of the trade-shock work and is left out only because of the three-name limit. She also notes that Katz's best-known education-technology work was with a recent laureate, so his credit is partly overlapping.
responses.response: This is the most important open question on B006, and I take it seriously. Dorn's claim on the China-shock papers is closer than Katz's. Katz's distinct contribution is the long-run skill-premium and wage-structure line, which predates and frames the task and trade work. Dorn is also younger, and the 2023 prize addressed a different question from the education-technology race. I still prefer Autor, Hanson and Katz, because the citation then covers both the technology and trade strands. If the Committee prefers a trade-shock-centred citation, Autor, Dorn and Hanson is a defensible substitution. I regard this as a real judgment call, not a settled point.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B004 first. He argues that nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework are the working core of modern monetary policy analysis, with very large impact on theory and practice, and that Taylor, Woodford and Calvo are the most separable contributors.
responses.response: I agree on the influence and maturity, which is why I rank B004 second. I part from Andersson on how well attribution can be resolved. Calvo's pricing device, Taylor's contracts and rule, and Woodford's synthesis are separable, but Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets built the empirical and estimated versions that made the framework usable. A trio would effectively write that second layer out of the citation. The post-2008 and 2021-23 debates also leave the framework's empirical standing less settled than the influence suggests. For me this tilts the choice toward B006, where the credit problem is smaller. I do not think it removes B004 from serious consideration.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B007 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) first. He argues it gives a unified framework for how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy, that its credit is comparatively clean, and that it complements the 2024 institutions prize without duplicating it.
responses.response: The cleanliness of attribution is a real strength, and it is better than for B006 or B004. I did not rank B007 in my opening eight, and the reason is scientific, not about field. Identification of constitutional and electoral-rule effects is weaker than in the design-based work in B006, and the headline empirical results are more sensitive to assumptions. I also see less direct evidence of impact on adjacent fields. I would revise this if colleagues can show that the empirical findings are robust across modern identification standards.

uncertainties: Whether Dorn should replace Katz, or whether a trade-shock-centred citation (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) would be more defensible than one spanning both technology and trade.
How much marginal weight to give B006 given adjacent recent prizes in labour economics, technology and institutions, and whether that affects timing as opposed to merit.
Persistence and magnitude of China-shock effects, and the inference properties of shift-share designs.
Whether the credit for the task framework, which includes Levy and Murnane outside the ballot, can be handled fairly by this citation.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent for the B006 laureates from the supplied profile. I have long-running collaborations with Per Krusell (committee secretary) and John Hassler (chair), and both are IIES colleagues. They are disclosed, not adjudicated. My regular co-authors Aghion, Bergeaud, Klenow and Li are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. My field proximity to growth, structural change and firm reallocation has been applied under the same criteria used for other fields.
